Regression Analysis Tables

Source: vignettes/articles/regression.qmd 
library(dplyr)
library(parameters)
library(performance)
library(apa7)
library(psych)

The apa7 package is closely aligned with the easystats suite of packages for reporting statistical analyses. In most cases, it relies on easystats functions to do most of the hard work and then converts the output to APA style tables. For example, the easystats package parameters has a function model_parameters that takes regression fit objects and displays regression coefficient tables into a tibble that is displayed as a markdown table. The apa_parameters function converts the output of model_parameters into a tibble that is ready for apa_flextable to display as an APA-style table. The workflow has three steps:

  1. Make a regression model fit object with lm, glm, or a similar function.
  2. apa_parameters converts the fit object into a tibble using easystats functions.
  3. apa_flextable converts the tibble into an APA-style table.

Because step 2 returns a tibble, you can post-process it with dplyr before step 3. In Quarto and R Markdown documents, however, the output of apa_parameters is displayed as an APA-style table automatically, so step 3 is only needed when you want to customize the table or save it.

Linear Regression 

d <- sat.act |>
  mutate(
    gender = factor(
      gender,
      levels = 1:2,
      labels = c("Male", "Female")
    ),
    education = factor(
      education,
      levels = 0:5,
      labels =     c("None", "High School", "Some College", "Bachelor", "Master", "Doctorate")
    )
  ) |>
  tidyr::drop_na()

lm1 <- lm(ACT ~ age + gender, d)
lm2 <- update(lm1, . ~ . + education)
lm3 <- update(lm2, . ~ . + SATV + SATQ)

In the console, apa_parameters prints as an ordinary tibble, so you can inspect it. Here as_tibble is used to show that tibble in this document.

apa_parameters(lm1) |>
  tibble::as_tibble()
# A tibble: 3 × 6
  Variable      `*B*` `*SE*` `&beta;` `*t*(684)` `*p*`

3 Gender–Female −0.40 0.38   −.04     −1.03       .30

Binary Logistic Regression

Psychologists who study volunteers have long worried that the people who sign up for experiments differ from the people who do not. If personality predicts who volunteers, findings from volunteer samples may not generalize. Cowles and Davis (1987) asked 1,421 students whether they would volunteer for a psychology experiment and measured their neuroticism and extraversion with the Eysenck Personality Inventory. The data are in the Cowles data set from the carData package.

Neuroticism and extraversion are centered at their means so that, when the model includes their interaction, each trait’s coefficient is its effect for a person of average standing on the other trait.

d_vol <- carData::Cowles |>
  mutate(
    Volunteer = volunteer == "yes",
    Sex = sex,
    Neuroticism = neuroticism - mean(neuroticism),
    Extraversion = extraversion - mean(extraversion)
  )

glm_vol1 <- glm(
  Volunteer ~ Sex + Neuroticism + Extraversion,
  data = d_vol,
  family = binomial
)

apa_parameters accepts glm objects. The table reports the coefficients on the log-odds scale (B), their standard errors, the exponentiated coefficients, and the test statistics. For logistic regression, the exponentiated coefficient is the odds ratio (OR), and the test statistic is z.

apa_parameters(glm_vol1)

Each odds ratio is the multiplicative change in the odds of volunteering for a one-point increase in the predictor (or, for Sex, for men compared with women), holding the other predictors constant. For the constant, the exponentiated coefficient is the odds of volunteering for a woman of average neuroticism and extraversion, not an odds ratio.

Exponentiated coefficients are added whenever the link function is logit or log. They are labeled OR for logit links, IRR (incidence rate ratio) for log links in count models, and RR (risk ratio) for log links in binomial models. Set exponentiate = FALSE to leave them out, or exponentiate = TRUE to add them for other links such as probit.

apa_parameters(glm_vol1, exponentiate = FALSE)

Comparing logistic regression models

Does the effect of extraversion depend on neuroticism? A second model adds their interaction. A list of glm models is displayed with a pseudo-R2 (Tjur’s for logistic regression, as chosen by performance::r2) and a likelihood ratio test of the change, because the binomial family has a fixed dispersion parameter.

glm_vol2 <- update(glm_vol1, . ~ . + Neuroticism:Extraversion)
apa_parameters(list(glm_vol1, glm_vol2))

The interaction improves the fit, but the gain in Tjur’s R2 is small. Its odds ratio is below 1: the more neurotic a person is, the less extraversion increases the odds of volunteering.

Printing Options

The apa7.print option controls how the output of apa_parameters, apa_performance, and apa_performance_comparison is displayed.

  • "auto" (default): table in Quarto and R Markdown documents, tibble in the console.
  • "flextable": table everywhere.
  • "tibble": tibble everywhere.
options(apa7.print = "flextable")

To get the table with non-default settings, pass the output to apa_flextable, which always returns a flextable.
